reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Multifocal disorder combining two or more of limbic encephalitis, brainstem encephalitis, cerebellar degeneration, myelitis, dorsal root ganglionopathy and autonomic failure.
Anti-Hu (ANNA-1) is the archetypal antibody, with small-cell lung carcinoma found in the large majority of cases.
Anti-CV2/CRMP5 disease may add chorea, optic neuritis and peripheral neuropathy to the picture.
Brainstem involvement produces vertigo, nystagmus, diplopia, dysarthria and dysphagia, and can threaten respiration.
Autonomic involvement is common and may manifest as gastrointestinal pseudo-obstruction from enteric neuronal loss, orthostatic hypotension or cardiac dysrhythmia.
Neurological symptoms usually antedate the cancer diagnosis and the underlying tumour is often small and limited-stage.
Response to immunotherapy is generally poor; prompt treatment of the tumour offers the best chance of neurological stabilisation.
CSF is usually inflammatory (pleocytosis, raised protein, oligoclonal bands) even when MRI is normal.
reference.pathophysiology: Tumour cells (most often small-cell lung carcinoma) express intracellular onconeural antigens such as HuD that are normally restricted to neurons. The resulting immune response is dominated by antigen-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes that infiltrate multiple levels of the neuraxis, producing perivascular inflammation, microglial nodules and neuronal loss in cortex, brainstem, cerebellum, spinal cord, dorsal root ganglia and autonomic ganglia. The detected antibodies (anti-Hu, anti-CV2/CRMP5, anti-amphiphysin) are useful diagnostic markers but are largely not directly pathogenic, which accounts for the poor reversibility.
additionalDifferentials: infectious rhombencephalitis (e.g. listerial) and other viral encephalomyelitides
multiple sclerosis or neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder
primary CNS lymphoma or leptomeningeal metastatic disease
vitamin B12 or vitamin E deficiency (subacute combined degeneration)
additionalInvestigations: serum and CSF anti-Hu (ANNA-1) and extended paraneoplastic antibody panel
MRI brain and whole spine with contrast
CSF analysis with cytology and oligoclonal bands
whole-body FDG-PET/CT and CT chest, with bronchoscopy if indicated
nerve conduction studies and EMG for associated neuronopathy
autonomic function testing and gastrointestinal transit studies
EEG when encephalopathy or seizures are present
redFlags: respiratory failure or bulbar compromise from brainstem involvement
newly identified malignancy requiring urgent staging
reference.prognosis: Neurological prognosis is generally poor; deficits often persist even when the tumour is controlled, although the disease may stabilise with effective oncological treatment. Paradoxically, anti-Hu-associated small-cell lung carcinoma is sometimes detected at a limited stage and may show relatively favourable tumour control.
pitfalls: Attributing multifocal neurological signs to cerebral metastases rather than a paraneoplastic process.
Discontinuing the tumour search after an initial negative imaging screen.
Underestimating autonomic involvement, which can be life-threatening.
Delaying oncological treatment while awaiting a neurological response to immunotherapy.
references: Graus F, Delattre JY, et al. Recommended diagnostic criteria for paraneoplastic neurological syndromes.
Dalmau J, Rosenfeld MR. Paraneoplastic syndromes of the CNS. Lancet Neurology.
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice, current edition.
